Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 349 Ungulate Aerial Survey (2018) 
 
 
Background 
The last survey conducted for a population estimate was in winter of 2012-13 using the random stratified block 
methodology. Since all surveys were conducted later in January/February when conditions were favourable, the 
ability to acquire meaningful age data (antler class) on moose at this time due to antler drop was difficult and 
therefore not reported.  
Antlered moose are managed on a limited entry hunt with an early (S24-O31) and late (N1-N30) season including 
an archery only season (A25-S23); there is no antlerless moose season. Antlered mule deer are also managed 
through a limited entry hunt (S17-N30) including a general archery only season (A25-S16); there is no antlerless 
mule deer season. White-tailed deer (antlered and antlerless) are managed by a general archery only season 
(A25-S16) and a general season (S17-N30); up until 2015 two supplemental antlerless tags could also be 
acquired. Since 2015 only one supplemental antlerless tag is valid within the WMU. Antlered elk are managed on a 
3-point general season (S17-N30) including a general archery only season (A25-S16); there is no antlerless elk 
season. 
 
Survey Method 
The objective of this survey was to establish a population estimate for moose; including age and sex classifications 
where possible. Transects, 10 km in length and oriented north-south, were established spatially throughout the 
WMU at 2 km intervals within a GIS environment. Based on previous moose survey densities, transects were 
randomly selected until 620 kilometres of survey distance was achieved, how ever an additional 220 kilometres of 
transect were flown to increase the sample size of observed moose. To help improve estimate precision, an 
attempt was made to spatially stratify the WMU into high and low density using habitat and landscape disturbance 
variables. Unfortunately, this desktop stratification was not helpful in the final analyses. The survey was then flown 
using distance sampling methodology as described in the Distance Sampling Chapter of the Aerial Ungulate 
Survey Protocol Manual (ESRD, 2014). 
 
Results 
This survey was completed from February 7-9, 2018 and included a total of 18.9 hours of rotor-wing effort. Total 
ungulates observed were 141 moose, 41 white-tailed deer, 6 mule deer and 1 elk observed from 99, 17, 1, and 1 
independent groups, respectively. Of the 141 moose that were successfully classified, 78 were cows, 25 were 
calves, and 37 were bulls; 68% of bulls observed had already shed there antlers, therefore size classifications 
could not be accurately determined. The observed sample corresponds to a WMU level population split: 626 bulls 
– 1320 Cows – 423 calves. Other ungulates were not encountered at reasonable densities to accurately report on 
population estimates or demographics. The current moose population estimate and density, including bull and calf 
ratios, are presented in Table 1 which includes historic survey estimates.
